analysis.one_liner: Taxes excess profits of large oil companies, taxes their stock buybacks, and ends a favored accounting method.
analysis.headline: Fourteen Senate Democrats backed the bill when it was introduced in August 2022, but it never received a committee vote before that Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 21% tax on "excess profits" — profits above a normal return — of large oil and gas companies through 2025. It would also charge those companies 25% of the value of any stock they buy back, and take away the LIFO accounting method, a bookkeeping rule that large oil companies can use to lower their taxable income. Companies under $1 billion in average annual receipts would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit through revenue raised from the temporary excess-profits and buyback taxes, which would flow to the Treasury. The bill was written in response to the 2022 spike in gas prices and record oil company profits, and its aim was to push back on that by taxing windfall gains and discouraging companies from spending profits on buybacks rather than on drilling or lowering prices. Consumers and retirement savers may also benefit indirectly if companies shift money away from buybacks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and drivers at the pump

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an additional 21% tax through 2025 on the profits of oil and gas companies with over $1 billion in average annual gross receipts that exceed a 'normal return' of 10% of gross receipts.

Charges publicly traded large oil and gas corporations an excise tax equal to 25% of the fair market value of any stock they buy back, which is designed to discourage companies from spending record profits on buybacks instead of other uses.
Ends the use of LIFO (last-in, first-out) inventory accounting for large oil and gas companies, which reduces the methods these companies can use to lower their reported taxable income.

Contains anti-avoidance rules aimed at pass-through entities, foreign subsidiaries importing oil into the United States, and corporate inversions, so that profits routed through other structures would still be taxed.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil and gas producers, refiners, processors, transporters, and distributors — the integrated majors and other companies with over $1 billion in average annual gross receipts. Their shareholders, including executives and large investors, would bear the tax directly or through reduced company value. Some economists argue such a tax can be passed to consumers at the pump through reduced supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big oil companies and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: Windfall profits taxes are temporary and unpredictable; critics argue they discourage investment in future oil and gas production, which could tighten supply and raise prices for consumers later — the opposite of the bill's goal of relief at the pump.

The excess-profits tax is computed on taxable income with a 10% normal-return threshold, and companies facing higher costs in a given year could owe the tax even when their real economic profits were ordinary; the refundable-computation rules add complexity for the IRS and companies alike.
The taxes and the LIFO change are temporary (ending after 2025), so they do not permanently restructure the industry's tax treatment, limiting the lasting benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a concentrated industry at a moment of record profits and high gas prices, and the buyback tax in particular directly discourages a use of profits that does nothing for consumers. The main honest cost is investment-discipline: a tax aimed at windfall profits can deter the very production that would bring prices down, and a temporary tax creates incentives to shift activity around it. On balance the provisions are narrow — large companies only, sunsetting in 2025 — which limits both the benefit and the risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2022 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Taxing Big Oil Profiteers Act on August 4, 2022, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors including Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate Majority Leader.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, where tax bills must first be approved before the full Senate can vote.
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies and their shareholders are better off: they avoided the excess-profits tax, the 25% buyback tax, and the loss of LIFO accounting that the bill would have imposed through 2025.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon and bill sponsor; Chair, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee, which he chaired, but never brought it to a committee markup or vote.

for.name: 13 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sen. Chuck Schumer (Majority Leader)

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with no action taken
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed windfall-profits taxes on oil companies during the 2022 price spike, arguing they would discourage investment in production.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans backed the bill; no vote was ever taken, so party positions were never recorded on the floor.

industries.industry: Large oil and gas producers, refiners, and distributors
industries.note: The bill layers a 21% excess-profits tax, a 25% buyback tax, and the loss of LIFO accounting onto companies with over $1 billion in annual receipts, directly cutting into record profits earned during the 2022 price spike. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against the bill's stated aim of relief for consumers and revenue for taxpayers.

industries.industry: Oil company executives and large shareholders
industries.note: The excess-profits computation denies deductions for nearly all employee compensation at covered companies and the buyback tax targets returns to shareholders, so executives and big investors would bear much of the cost directly.

industries.industry: Small oil and gas companies (under $1 billion in annual receipts)
industries.note: The bill exempts companies below the $1 billion gross-receipts threshold from all three provisions, sparing them the taxes competitors would pay — a relative advantage, though a minor one for most small operators.
